summary: Contains the text of a statement signed on 29 August 2012 by the IEEE Standards Association, the IAB, the IETF, the Internet Society and the W3C. It affirms a set of principles, known as OpenStand, for open, jointly developed global standards. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Several big groups that make rules for the internet signed a note together saying how good rules should be made: openly, fairly, and with everyone invited.

questions: what are the modern paradigm for standards principles
subtitle: A joint statement on principles for open, global standards development.

tldr.problem: Standards organizations needed a shared understanding of how modern global standards should be developed to ensure they are fair, open, and benefit the whole internet ecosystem.
tldr.mechanism: Five major standards bodies—IEEE-SA, IAB, IETF, ISOC, and W3C—jointly signed the OpenStand affirmation, endorsing five principles for standards development.
tldr.outcome: The OpenStand principles provide a framework for how standards organizations should operate: with cooperation, due process, transparency, balance and openness.

today: RFC 6852 is an Informational RFC published by the Internet Architecture Board. The OpenStand principles remain the shared framework for how the internet's major standards organizations conduct their work.

sections.title: The OpenStand Affirmation
sections.content:
On 29 August 2012, the leaders of five major standards organizations signed a joint statement: the IEEE Standards Association, the Internet Architecture Board (IAB), the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), the Internet Society (ISOC), and the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). They affirmed a set of principles for how modern, global standards should be developed. These principles became known as OpenStand.

The affirmation recognizes that the internet's explosive growth and success came from standards that were developed openly, with broad participation, and voluntarily adopted based on technical merit.
sections.plainLanguage: The big leaders of internet standards organizations sat down and agreed on the right way to make standards: openly and fairly.

sections.title: The Five Principles
sections.content:
The OpenStand framework rests on five principles that standards organizations should follow:

Due process: Decisions are made fairly, with no single party dominating, processes are transparent, and there are ways to appeal. Standards are reviewed and updated on a schedule.

Broad consensus: All views are considered so that agreement can be found across different interests.

Transparency: Organizations announce their work in advance, make decisions publicly, and allow comment periods before final approval.

Balance: No single person, company, or interest group exclusively controls standards activities.

Openness: Standards processes are open to all interested and informed parties.

A sixth commitment, voluntary adoption, means standards succeed based on market demand, not mandate. Standards must also be available to implement under fair terms—ranging from royalty-free to fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory licensing.
sections.plainLanguage: Good rules are made when everyone can speak, nobody dominates, everything is transparent, and people are free to use them or not.

sections.title: The OpenStand Commitment
sections.content: RFC 6852 published the signed affirmation as a permanent record. The five signatory organizations committed to building standards that drive global competition, enable innovation, and support interoperability across the internet ecosystem. The statement invited other organizations, governments, and corporations worldwide to publicly endorse the principles at open-stand.org.
sections.plainLanguage: They promised to follow these ideas, and invited everyone else to promise the same.
